utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just before we continue where we left off yesterday, just one quick question on Sarvas and Aljmas. In those two villages there were no military -- JNA facilities or barracks; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You don't --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you yesterday I have never visited either Sarvas or Aljmas or whatever those places are called, so don't ask me about things I have no knowledge of. I really have no knowledge of any military facilities, whether they were there or not, but I do know that these places were taken by the paramilitary units of Croatia and that from those positions they were threatening members of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We stopped yesterday, we had discussed the -- the Presidency session of the 12th to 15th March 1991, and we had established and read from Mr. Jovic's book that, except for Mr. Jovic himself and Mr. Jugoslav Kostic, nobody agreed to declare a state of emergency, and the question now was did they vote and for what did they vote? And I would like to return to Mr. Jovic's book to clarify that situation. It's again what we have already quoted from yesterday. It's from his book, the entry of the 12th of March, 1991, and it says at the very end of this remark in the book, it says: "The following voted for this edited version of the decision without imposing of a state of emergency and with raising the military combat readiness and additional mobilisation," and that's the vote that they actually took. It's not about state of emergency but raising the military combat readiness and additional mobilisation. And it's actually here that Mr. Bucin, Mr. Sapundzija, Jugoslav Kostic and Jovic voted for it, and Mr. Bogicevic, Stjepan Mesic, and Vasil Tupurkovski against. So I think that clarifies also the question of Judge Kwon and you, your own memory of that someone voted; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, I have to correct you. Yesterday you did state what you are saying today but I did not confirm it. All I said was that I did not attend that session and that I watched the television footage of that session several times. The vast majority of my people and I still believe that at that session in March, Bogic Bogicevic voted for the proclamation of a state of emergency, so that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. I mean, we went through the book and you have already said you weren't there, so we'll leave it at that. I will now move on to the speech --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you tried to say this as if I had confirmed it, and I did not confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kostic. I said that it was in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, is there not a formal record of the vote?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: There is -- there is no formal record of the vote. We actually -- as far as I know, there isn't, but I will check it in the break. I don't think we have any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, yesterday you were already discussing with Mr. Milosevic or, rather, a few days before you discussed with Mr. Milosevic Exhibit 333, tab 51, the Politika article with the speech of Mr. Milosevic that he gave on the 16th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for your notice, it's also Exhibit 328, tab 29. We had it already earlier as a video.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to quote from that speech, and you can actually use tab -- Mr. Kostic, you can use tab D -- tab 51 in your binders.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we have page 2? We need page 2. Page 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's -- the English translation is two pages, the Serbian is just one page. In the English, Your Honours, it's page 2, on top of this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we have here what Mr. Milosevic said, and I quote: "Taking the newly emerged situation into consideration, I want to announce that the Republic of Serbia will not recognise any decisions reached by the SFRY Presidency because under existing circumstances any such decision would be illegitimate. I will not accept any transfer of authority in accordance with the constitution of Yugoslavia from Borisav Jovic to myself in case of his resignation in the work of such Presidency that has chosen to advocate disintegration of Yugoslavia. I expect that citizens of Serbia, Yugoslavia, and world opinion will understand that no patriot can accept the legitimacy of a president of a state who acts against his own country and constitution. "I demand that the Assembly of the Republic of Serbia, in accordance with the act on the takeover of authority from the Kosovo Assembly, reach a decision on the release of Riza Sapundzija from his duty as a member of the SFRY Presidency on their next session." Mr. Kostic, and that did happen, did it? Mr. Riza Sapundzija was dismissed by the Serbian Assembly; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And he continues, Mr. Milosevic continues: "Under existing circumstances of attempts to set off violence in Sandzak and Kosovo and Metohija, I have ordered a mobilisation of reserve Republic of Serbia MUP security forces and urgent establishment of additional police forces of the Republic of Serbia. I ask the government of the Republic of Serbia to carry out necessary preparations for the establishment of the additional forces in number that would guarantee protection of interest of the Republic of Serbia and the Serbian people." Mr. Kostic, that's what Mr. Milosevic said, and these additional police forces, they were established, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't give you any specific details, but I do think that the numbers of police were increased in Serbia. This was in the direct purview of the Ministry of the Interior and therefore the president of the Republic of Serbia in this particular case. These were the police forces of Serbia, not the federal police force. The police force of Serbia. And it was the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia as a federal unit that was in charge of that. What you have just read, I will take the liberty of commenting upon it. You see, all the members of the Presidency of the SFRY after the session in March and the impossibility of accepting the decisions of the General Staff, they all resigned. Only Mesic, Drnovsek, Bogicevic and Tupurkovski remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I thought you would comment on the question that I put but I see you are commenting on something different, so I want you to return to my question. You have to -- I have to tell you that because you have already -- we have already discussed here, and Mr. Milosevic did, what happened on that day. There's no need to repeat that. My question was about the additional police forces, and my further question in relation to that is: These additional police forces, they were established and they had different names, such as 1st, then Frenki's Red Berets, and finally Units for Special Operations. Isn't that so? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what you say. I don't know anything about this, either about the names or anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself were then elected to the Presidency, but your election to the Presidency was not supported by your own party. They didn't support you, did they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you got this information. It was my own party that nominated me to the Presidency. And in the Assembly of Montenegro, my party had a two-thirds majority, and it was the Assembly that elected me to that post. I don't know where you get this information that my party did not support me. Maybe you found a part in my book which says that when nominations to the Presidency were being considered, the top leadership of my party did not put my name forward at the time. But in the Assembly of Montenegro, my party had a two-thirds majority, and I was elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually had asked you that you were not supported by your party leadership and you just confirmed that. You wrote it in your book. You just confirmed that; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said my party did not support me. I only said that the top leadership, that is the Executive Board of my party, did not nominate me at that time. They nominated me to some other post. But my party did support me.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to exhibit this part of the book, and Ms. Dicklich is now bringing around -- handing out the part of the book. It's from Mr. Kostic's book, "Not To Be Forgotten," and it's page 267, 268, 269, and 207.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, as you know your book, I think I can continue with what's written in the book.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Muslim Assembly member also protested, as you describe in the book, against your nomination, and he actually does this because of, as he says, an anti-Muslim statement of yours. That's in your book, too; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in relation to the Muslim nation, as we are at that, your position was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There was no answer to that question. Is that in your book?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, he said actually yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, it's not on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please speak so that we can hear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in my book, but the lady did not mention the explanation, that it was a complete misinterpretation of my attitudes towards the Muslims. I think she should quote the entire passage. It does say in the book that the Muslim representative opposed my election, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I -- the Judges can read these passages for themselves. That's why I did not quote at all from the book, because you remembered it very well. And my question to you was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, please. Excuse me. Judges, may I intervene? If the representative of the Prosecution states here in public that I have anti-Muslim stances, that's a serious accusation and it's misinformation. If she quotes only a single book -- sentence from the book that I wrote without providing the explanation, then it takes on a completely different meaning. That's why I ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one of two things. We can either decide to -- to have you provide the additional information, or Mr. Milosevic can raise it in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honour -- Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I also only quoted or referred to this Muslim member saying that; I did not say that this was for a fact. I just mentioned that the Muslim member said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic may take this up in re-examination if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just understand what I have said. Just understand what I have said. This is -- I understand what you have said, and Mr. Milosevic may raise it in re-examination. So the matter will be dealt with. There's no need to continue the discussion. Please continue. I have said that you are -- you are not to interrupt. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in relation to the Muslim nation, your position was that the Muslims are not really a nation like the Serbs or the Croats. Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you are showing a total lack of knowledge in this area if you can say something like that. You're quoting part of my book, so you probably will have read what Their Honours would not allow me to read. If you are now saying that I do not recognise the Muslims as a nation, then you are either misinformed or malicious, because you fail to distinguish between people and nation; "narod" and "nacija." When Their Honours asked me who the constituent nations of Yugoslavia were, I said a few days ago that these were Slovenians, Croats, Montenegrins, Macedonians, Serbs, and so on, and then I said that after 1962 or 1965, I'm not exactly sure when, my party, the League of Communists, which had a one-party monopoly, recognised to the Muslims in Yugoslavia the name of a nation and constituent nation based purely on religion. Anyone with any knowledge of this area has to draw a distinction between the term "narod," or people, and "nacija," nationality. Nations and nationalities. Muslim people are very numerous in Montenegro. Ever since I was a child I have associated with Muslims, but these are two completely different concepts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not need that much detail. You were elected by the Montenegrin government in April 1991 for this position in the Presidency, but your post was only confirmed in mid-May. There was a problem in the SFRY Assembly because of the fact that the Serbian Assembly had elected Sejdo Bajramovic and the SFRY Assembly refused to ratify the new members because of that fact. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, first of all, it was not the government of Montenegro that elected me but the parliament of Montenegro, to my position in the Presidency. It's true that in the Assembly of the SFRY there was a problem in verifying the election of Sejdo Bajramovic and Mr. Jugoslav Kostic, both of them, because they were elected by the Assembly of Serbia, as far as I know in accordance with the constitution of Serbia, but the separatist leaderships of Slovenia and Croatia were already attempting to disrupt and to support every measure taken in the provinces that would make it easier for them to carry out their secession.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it's a fact that there was a problem in particular with Mr. Sejdo Bajramovic, because he did not represent the interest of the Kosovo Assembly but the interest of the Serbian Assembly; right? That was the point that was made in relation to him. Is that --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Sejdo Bajramovic and Mr. Jugoslav Kostic were in the same position. There was no reason --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's enough. Thank you. Mr. Kostic, from mid-May until June 1992 onwards, you participated not only in the work of the SFRY Presidency but in addition you also met with members of the Serbian and Montenegrin leadership and the leadership of the JNA outside of Presidency meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, to be sure. Not just with them. I met with many people with whom I had a common stance to preserve Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to hand to the parties and to Mr. Kostic a table produced by the Office of the Prosecutor. So that's easier for us to have now further questions. This is actually an overview of meetings between the SFRY Presidency and military between May 1991 and May 1992, and it's actually based on Mr. Jovic's book "Last Days of the SFRY." Mr. Kostic, these are, of course, only those meetings that Mr. Jovic mentioned in the book. I assume that in addition to that you probably had a lot more meetings.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And what am I supposed to say about this table? Do you think I can remember every meeting?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no. You're not expected to remember them all. We will go through a very few. But it just mentions here, when you look at the total figures, that, in the book of Mr. Jovic, you participate in 21 of these meetings with the military and Mr. Bulatovic actually 15 times. And as I said, I assume you probably met much more often than Mr. Jovic mentioned. Could that be right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt it. I would rather believe that you added something than took away, but we had daily meetings, madam. The situation was dramatic. The country was falling apart. There were clashes. There was a war on. We sat at meetings all day long. So don't expect me to confirm for each and every one of these that that was exactly when the meeting was held. You can see that Mr. Jovic attended most of these. Well, of course. He was in the Presidency before I was appointed to the Presidency and elected vice-president of the Presidency. You mention meetings with a Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Jovic. Well, of course. I've already said that I can't know to what extent Mr. Jovic communicated with Mr. Milosevic, but I assume it was very often, which is only natural because he was representing Serbia in the highest state organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are meant to demonstrate meetings which involved the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What significance, then, has a meeting where neither the military representatives mentioned was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, this chart does not only refer to meetings with the military. It also - and you will hear from further questions - it relates actually to a group of people that would meet frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Kostic, as you have read Mr. Jovic's book, Mr. Jovic refers to a group of six people or, rather, he says the six men, and he means he himself, Mr. Jovic, Milosevic, Bulatovic, the Generals Kadijevic and Adzic, and actually you yourself. Do you -- are you aware that he is speaking of these six men?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice the term "group" used, but according to the names you've just read out of those people, it was a team. That was the composition of the people who at the time represented the top-most representatives of Serbia and Montenegro in the republics in the SFRY Presidency and the top representatives of the General Staff. But I didn't ever notice the term "group" used. Perhaps what you keep saying in the indictment as a joint criminal enterprise, perhaps you're alluding to something like that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I just said that Mr. Jovic didn't use the word "the group." I use it. He says the six men, and we can also stick to this word.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, just to your question, we actually have looked at these six men, and this chart relates to the six men and shows meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The title, then, is misleading, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, because it only speaks of meetings between the Presidency and the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The title is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I just want to refer to one of these meetings, and this is actually a meeting of the 14th of August, 1991, and it's mentioned in Exhibit 596, tab 1, the 89(F) statement of Mr. Jovic. If you look at paragraph 87, it says here: "A meeting took place at Kadijevic's on 14 August 1991. The meeting was attended by Kadijevic, Adzic, Milosevic, Bulatovic, Kostic and I." "I," that's Mr. Jovic. "We received information on the military situation in the field on, inter alia, the Krajina and Slavonia. Kadijevic told us about the discord among the Serbs in Krajina and Slavonia in both the political and military sense. Individuals like Kostic were giving statements without consultation in opposition to the views of the military," and so on and so forth. "Coordination was urgently necessary among the six. Kadijevic proposed the idea of an expert staff (larger group than the six). The idea of systematic consultation by the six was accepted but not the idea of Mr. Kadijevic." Do you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, the meeting held by Mr. Jovic I don't remember in particular because we had many similar meeting of that kind, but what you've just read out here, I have no reason to challenge it. All I can say is that it is quite possibly correct. I know that at times I was -- my name came up in the mass media fairly often, and my statements did, too, but there was a complete disorientation among the people at the time, and that's what I say in my book; that Mr. Milosevic, for example, on one occasion when we talked over the telephone said, "Well, Branko, you're in the media too much. Your name appears there too much." And I said, "Well, thank you, Mr. Milosevic, I think you crop up in the media perhaps too fewer times." But any way, I said during my present testimony that we didn't think alike on all matters, and in the previous days testifying here, I mentioned my divergencies with Mr. Jovic, for example, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just let me lead you back to what we are actually talking about. The meeting of the 14th of August of 1991, you say you don't remember it. However, it seems, at least according to what Mr. Jovic remembered, that you, and I think it's meant probably you, "Individuals like Kostic were giving statements without consultation in opposition to the views of the military." This criticism, was that because of what you said in your visit in Borovo Selo? Do you remember the criticism that was voiced here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think - as far as I know, at least - that I did not have a single criticism coming at me from the most responsible people in the army right up until the pensioning off of the second group of generals in May 1992. So there were no criticisms either from Mr. Veljko Kadijevic or Mr. Blagoje Adzic either in the sense of saying that my public statements differed from the positions taken by the army. I never had any criticisms of that nature. That's one point. Now, secondly, as far as my visit to Borovo Selo goes, that could have certainly not been a reason for Jovic's statement, because I visited Borovo Selo after having consulted the other members of the Presidency of the SFRY, and I considered that I, as a representative of Montenegro in the Presidency, was better placed to go to Borovo Selo than a representative of Serbia, for example, the Serbian representative in the Presidency to go to Borovo Selo, because we didn't view that as Serbia's problem but as a problem for the whole of Yugoslavia. And our divergencies and parting of ways over certain other questions related to the involvement and engagement of the Yugoslav People's Army to deblock the barracks in Croatia under siege --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. We was talking about the Borovo Selo visit. When you were in Borovo Selo, you actually spoke to the local Serb audience and you did mention "an army of ours" when you spoke to the Serbs. You were asking for "an army of ours," didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our army. That's what I'm saying now, our army, the Yugoslav People's Army. And I was the vice-president and member of the Supreme Command, the Supreme Command in charge of the army. It was our army. And I have to say it was the best and -- best organised army --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... let me interrupt you here.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we come to what was said in Borovo Selo a little bit later.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic also wrote a book and in his book about the meeting of the 14th of August, 1991. Do you know Mr. Bulatovic's book "Rules of Silence"? Mr. Kostic, do you know that book?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that book. And I read the first 114 pages of the book by Momir Bulatovic, because they relate to the time when we worked together on -- holding various political and public functions. And in my new book that is called "Records," I give a critical appraisal -- I believe you have that book of mine -- but I gave a critical appraisal of that portion of Momir Bulatovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I -- I want to quote here about the meeting of the 14th of -- 14th October -- no. No, it says here -- oh, no, sorry. It's 14th October.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite another matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to quote, nevertheless, because it's a similar meeting to the one that Mr. Jovic is talking about, and I would like to have it in front of everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we have to put it on the ELMO. I just hear that we don't have it available for everyone. I would like to have the English on the ELMO, and for Mr. Jovic the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He speaks here in his book about the meeting of the 14th of October and Mr. Milosevic is present, Mr. Jovic is present, a member of the SFRY Presidency, Montenegrin side, Branko Kostic, Mile Djukanovic, and he says the following: "All of our talks, especially my numerous meetings with Slobodan Milosevic before this and in all the coming years, went by the same atmosphere. The meetings were intimate with completely open conversation. One used ordinary vocabulary and discussed every problem, including the hardest, while making references to various affairs and current jokes. In other words, one could feel that we were on the same team and sharing the same fate, regardless of all the differences ..." And it also continues then a little bit further down: "The meetings were almost never recorded (or it was not done in a way that I could notice). Official notes were rarely taken. Statements were issued in connection with certain meetings. The statements would be prepared by Mr. -- by Milosevic's chef de cabinet. By default, it was Milosevic and me who would edit the text of such a statement, or rewrite it." Do you recall this meeting or these kind of meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that particular meeting extremely well, and what Mr. Bulatovic said was correct. Now, as far as the other observations are concerned by Mr. Bulatovic, I really don't wish to comment on them because the comments about that meeting you could also find in my book. And I do believe you have it, I don't suppose you've skipped it over. It was a consultation that we held right before The Hague Conference was due to take place, which met at the -- on the 18th of October, and this was on the 14th of October. Now, the simple question arose of what we should do faced with a situation of that kind, because we were dissatisfied with the proposal that had been made, the draft Hague document. And at this point in time, all I can tell you is -- and I don't wish, madam, either Mr. Bulatovic -- to criticise or denounce any of my fellow citizens or Mr. Bulatovic in any way, but you have had a chance to talk to Mr. Bulatovic, or can have one, and I wrote a critical appraisal about the book of Mr. Bulatovic. In my new book called "Records" or "Zapisnik," you will be able to find that critical appraisal in my book, and I say at the end of it that that critical appraisal of the book I am writing for the sole reason that I want to say that certain statements by Mr. Bulatovic have to be taken with a pinch of salt, or with reservations, because they're not all correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I am -- I will speak with you about this particular meeting and in particular the October situation and the Carrington Plan later in the cross-examination, so we don't need to go into details of that meeting from the substance, but what Mr. Bulatovic is actually speaking about is a group of people sharing the same fate - that's how he puts it - "sharing the same fate regardless of differences." This sharing the same fate, does that relate to the political survival of the Serbian and Montenegrin leadership?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give a comment here and an interpretation of what Mr. Bulatovic meant when he said that. I can just assume that Mr. Bulatovic meant that we shared the same convictions and that we're making the same efforts and had the same desire to preserve Yugoslavia, because in my testimony so far, I have said that although we had differences, what united us, the basic fact that united us and kept us rallied together was this desire to preserve Yugoslavia and to resolve our political crisis in a peaceful manner. Now, the fact that he mentions these six people, I've already said they were the most responsible leaders of Serbia and Montenegro. One was the Prime Minister, the other one was the president of the state, one in Serbia, one in Montenegro, and both Jovic and I were members of the Yugoslav state Presidency from those two republics. Kadijevic and Adzic were the two most responsible men in the army, the top leaders. And of all the institutions in Yugoslavia, the army was most fervently in favour of the preservation of Yugoslavia. So I think that Mr. Bulatovic meant that, the preservation of Yugoslavia, not the preservation of power.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From March onwards, the political survival of the leaderships in Serbia and Montenegro and also the JNA, but closely linked to the fate of the Serbs in Croatia, was it is not? Assisting the Serbs in Croatia assisted the survival of these leaderships; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you on that point. Through force of circumstance, it was all about the Serbs in Croatia. However, in all our statements, both in my statements and the statements of all the other six people that you mention in this context, you'll always find our readiness and duty to perform our constitutional functions pursuant to the constitution, letter of the constitution, and if necessary, with the Yugoslav People's Army to give physical protection to every nation or part of a nation that could physically be under jeopardy. I said that in Borovo Selo, and you have what I said there. I said that the units of the Yugoslav People's Army would be deployed the same way to provide defence and protection to our Muslims and Albanians and our Macedonians had they been under threat as the Serbs in Croatia were. So it was through force of circumstance in this instance it was the Serbs in Croatia that were physically under jeopardy, so I think that your interpretation of that is erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I was going to ask you what is your specific answer to the question, but you have now given it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me now turn again to Exhibit -- the exhibit, statement of Mr. Jovic. That is Exhibit 596, tab 1, 89(F) statement of Mr. Jovic, and it's now paragraph 74 and 75. And it relates to April 1991 in his book. And 75 I just quote from so you get the context. It's Mr. Milosevic, Kadijevic, and Adzic and Jovic actually talking about the situation in Croatia and the JNA involvement. It says here, and I quote, rather, from the end of paragraph 74: "We asked them whether the military would allow the Croatian police to occupy Knin and other Serb cities, which are now under Serb control. The response was very clear; no." And I continue with paragraph 75: "It was decided that in the event that the Croats attack them, they would take armed action and notify me and I would then convene the Presidency and simply inform them of the fact. I was not prepared to seek any decision or consent. Milosevic and I drew their attention to the fact that only -- that only other approach would be betrayal, and that in this case betrayal means the fall of the Serbian leadership and the collapse of the JNA." This is what Mr. Jovic says. He connects the fate of the Serbian leadership very closely with the actions to be taken to assess the Serbs in Croatia. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I think you are wasting time without purpose. The conversation that you mentioned was taking place at the time that I wasn't in the Presidency, and I sincerely hope that I and my position you are not taking as being the same as the position of the Serb government and Serb leadership. I was the Montenegrin representative there and I am a Montenegrin. Now, with respect to your last question, I have already given you an answer when I answered your last question. As far as I'm concerned, it was a constitutional duty both of the Yugoslav People's Army and the entire Presidency and not only Mr. Jovic or Branko Kostic, but it was the duty of all Presidency members, the constitutional duty to take into account the interests of all the citizens of the SFRY. We weren't representatives of only our own republics, and that was one of the main criticisms of having Mesic elected as president of the Presidency, because it was our duty --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, let me interrupt you. You answered my question, and it was very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Can I ask Professor Kostic at this moment the role of the president of Serbia and Montenegro in terms of -- in relation to the matters of the federal state. You referred to the six men as a team. Why should Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bulatovic participate in those talks? Once you said that Mr. Milosevic has nothing to do with the -- Mr. Jovic. He has no influence over Mr. Jovic, as Mr. Bulatovic has none over you. Why should they participate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, that's not what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could clarify, explain that matter to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kwon, first of all, I have to correct you. I never said - and not here either - that Mr. Jovic did not have any communication with Mr. Milosevic. I never said that. What I said was that I don't know how far those communications were frequent ones, but that I can assume that because Jovic held the most responsible post in the federal state and Milosevic was the president of Serbia, then I can only assume that their communication was frequent. I never said that they didn't communicate between themselves. That's one point. Secondly, in the same way, you could put the following question, but yes, I'll answer your direct question in just a moment. Do you really think, Mr. Kwon, that Mr. Mesic, for example, and Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Kucan and Mr. Drnovsek and Mr. Izetbegovic, wasn't that a team? Do you really think they didn't communicate amongst themselves and decide what they were going to do? Well, Mesic in his book writes about this very fact. He says that after the 1st of October meeting of the Presidency at which we assess that the country was in a situation of imminent threat of war, directly criticised Bogicevic and Tupurkovski for having come to the meeting at all, for having been present at the meeting. And he didn't dwell there. He sent a letter to Alija Izetbegovic and Kiro Gligorov and asked them not to attend any Presidency meetings further, that is to say Tupurkovski and Bogicevic, that they shouldn't attend any other meetings. Milosevic as president of Serbia and Bulatovic as president of the Montenegrin state Presidency didn't arrive at that post and function drop out from the sky. They were elected by the people democratically at legitimate elections. And those people were -- the people were represented through their government, through the parliament, through their state functionaries, and those people expressed the constant desire to preserve Yugoslavia. So it was quite natural that they had to be interested in preserving and protecting the interests of the people they represent. I don't know whether that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As at the beginning of your testimony in the context of changes in Montenegro in 1988, you said that Mr. Milosevic was regarded as a person who would be able to make things move.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's at T-47614 to 47615 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic was a charismatic leader, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And people would look up to him and expect leadership from him; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we're going to portray the atmosphere amongst the people at that time, I have to say that Mr. Milosevic was given broad support from all the social strata of society down to the last worker and cleaner on the street. His pictures were carried everywhere, posters of him were put up everywhere, although at that same time when people publicly acclaimed him most, I as president of the Presidency of Montenegro said publicly that I don't like that kind of iconography, and I stated publicly when they asked me as president of Montenegro what I thought about the fact that from the city buses they had removed pictures of Slobodan Milosevic from the buses going to Malesija, which is the Albanian national minority in Montenegro in Podgorica, I said that that was quite normal, as far as I'm concerned, if those pictures and photographs created disquiet among those people then, then it was quite normal that they would be taken off the buses, the pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, people saw in Mr. Milosevic the protector of the Serbs in Kosovo and Serbs outside Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. Not only that. I -- well, all right. Let me give you my intimate thoughts and how I view this matter subjectively. Many attempted to attack Mr. Milosevic at the time, and they do so today, as being a nationalist, an extreme nationalist. Now, I think that was quite wrong, if I might state my opinions. I think that Mr. President Milosevic for a long time, and I think has retained those communist convictions to the present day, according to which from a rather quagmire atmosphere that existed in the 1990s throughout the Yugoslav territory if we take into account and add to that the very difficult economic situation and the crisis that I talked about at the beginning of my testimony here, then I feel that many people, a large number of people saw in Milosevic a young, dynamic politician who would introduce a breath of fresh air into the country and a more dynamic process in the country. That is my personal opinion and conviction.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You just --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And if I might be allowed to add this: From that vast majority of people who at that time gave their undivided support to Milosevic, already at that time in my interview to the newspaper Borba - and I assume you have that because you've already quoted certain portions from that as president of the Presidency of Montenegro - I said there was a very broad spectrum and circle of people who give Milosevic their undivided support but time would tell very soon that there would be a stratification in that same corpus of men supporting Milosevic at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: As you already mentioned now the communist convictions, the military leadership saw in Mr. Milosevic the keeper of the socialists, the SFRY; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you would have to ask the military leadership about that. I can tell you by the same token that, regardless of all that we've been through, as an intellectual and a university professor, I have also preserved some of my socialist convictions because I believe some of that, some elements of that teaching is good for the entire humanity.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, would you agree that in every sense Mr. Milosevic was the key figure and main actor in Serbia and among the Serbs outside of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that Mr. Milosevic was the strongest political authority and had the greatest political influence, but I can say that about the territory of Serbia, and partly Montenegro. However, it would be completely wrong to say -- and I'm saying that with full responsibility: It is completely wrong to say that Mr. Milosevic had unfettered influence on the leaderships of Serbs outside Serbia. And if you want specific examples to illustrate this, I can provide them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We come to these examples later on. Just some more questions about Mr. Milosevic. Would you agree that he made decisions at times without consulting those who would usually be involved in decision-making?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never in a position to feel that personally, because I was never part of any leadership that included Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic was a leader of his own party in Serbia, which enjoyed the support of two-thirds of the parliament. He was the president of Serbia and held the highest post, and I was not in a position to feel it directly. But if you want my sincere and honest opinion, when at a debate in Pancevo that was organised by the opposition parties - and Pancevo is a small town near Belgrade - I was invited to that debate. As I used to do, I responded to such invitations from all parties, and that was in March 1992. They asked me what I thought about Milosevic. So at that time when Milosevic indubitably had the greatest authority, I didn't mince words. I said every tree has branches and every person has failings. Now, to answer your question directly: It is true that some people were replaced from the leadership overnight, and that is one of my main objections towards Mr. Milosevic. Although the later course of events in what is happening on the political arena of Serbia, what has been happening ever since Mr. Milosevic is not president, convinces me evermore that in territories that had not had democracy for a long time, democracy cannot flourish overnight.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Kostic, let me interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you do tend to go on too long. You are the kind of witness that has to be reined in and that has to be done either by the person questioning you or by me. If Mr. Milosevic was not the key figure among Serbs outside Serbia, then can you tell me who was in relation to each of the republics, starting with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we took it in chronology, we should start with Knin Krajina, but if you want me to start with Bosnia, I'll do that. I think the key political figure in Bosnia was Mr. Radovan Karadzic. In the military sense, the key figure was General Ratko Mladic. That's indisputable. Although I personally think that the leadership of Bosnian Serbs, ideologically and politically speaking, was a very diverse group, but they put the interests of the Serbian people first and put on the back burner all their political and ideological differences. They worked as team, and I think Mrs. Plavsic was an exception, because in many situations she was very extreme, especially in some situations when peaceful solutions were sought. In the Knin Krajina, there were two key political figures, and that is where we should look for a reason that caused eventually the tragedy of the Serb people in the Krajinas. The people were divided politically and ideologically at the time -- at a time when they should have been busy defending their homes. Mr. Robinson, I'm sorry, but these questions cannot be answered in one sentence. If you wanted an explanation, then I would appreciate it if you could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... very short explanation after you were given the names. In the Knin Krajina, you said there were two key political figures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The most influential two persons in the Knin Krajina in the period when I was in the Presidency of the SFRY, 1991 and the first half of 1992, were Milan Babic and Milan Martic. Before that the most influential person was Dr. Jovan Raskovic. However, this rift between Babic and Martic was not based on their personal differences. It was an ideological rift. The followers of Babic were practically supporters of the Chetnik ideology.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which next republic? I said the Republic of Serbian Krajina, I said about the Serb Republic in Bosnia. Which other republic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you have covered them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see that as part of one whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you agree that Mr. Milosevic personally decided on the elections for people for official positions? He took great interest and great influence there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't confirm that. I can assume that he did have influence, at least on some of those people if not all. But I cannot confirm one way or another.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff did not explain where. She didn't specify where I had influence, and Mr. Kostic is giving an answer thinking of Serbia, whereas she has been talking for a while implying Krajina and Bosnia, in which case the answers would be different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a fair point, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Where specifically are you speaking of?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was first speaking, actually, of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I would like to put something to you from a book that Mr. Jovic wrote, and that's the book on -- he simply calls it "Book On Milosevic."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put something from this, and Your Honour, it's Exhibit 596, tab 3, it is page 29 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I quote now from Mr. Jovic's book. By the way, do you know this book, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there is a book about Milosevic. I haven't read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "Milosevic's pretensions to conduct an absolutist policy concerning the cadre were not constrained only within the borders of Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in other words, to its organs. It included anyone who was not obedient enough and whose political destiny he could influence in any, even the slightest, degree. In order to suppress Milan Babic, the then president of the Government of --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The interpreter said absolutist policy. I think "policija," meaning "police," instead of "policy." The interpretation heard on the broadcast was that I was leading some sort of absolutist police, whereas it should be absolutist policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the English -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that's what I heard, "policy."

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's what we actually said, Mr. Milosevic. The word we said here is "the absolutist policy concerning the cadre." That's what I was quoting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I continue: "In order to suppress Milan Babic, the then president of the government of the RSK, who opposed his views, he publicly announced that he was severing any cooperation with the RSK until it elected another leadership, and then, via various forms of political malpractice, he made it happen." Mr. Kostic, that indeed is correct, what Mr. Jovic wrote here. That's what happened when Mr. Babic did not want to accept the Vance Plan; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I advise you to talk to Mr. Jovic about those things as long as you are quoting him. My views are completely different. It is my conviction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think there are issues of fact there. I mean, can you confirm that Mr. Milosevic publicly announced that he was severing cooperation with Republic of the Serbian Krajina until it elected another leadership?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure that that was definitively communicated that way, but I know that Mr. Milosevic did write a public, open letter to Milan Babic at the time, and its very sharp tone came as a surprise to the general public. However, I see that quite differently from Mr. Jovic. Mr. Babic was a supporter of a policy oriented to war, and he thought that all parts of Yugoslavia should get implicated in a war in Croatia and face the Croatian army, which was by that time much stronger and numerous than our Yugoslav People's Army, rather than negotiate with Europe, whereas we advocated the peace option, and we said the Vance Plan is the peace option. And that was the main reason for the disagreements and differences not only between Babic and Milosevic but also between me and Babic. I didn't agree with him either.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I was not talking about a letter, this exchange of letters between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Babic. I was actually asking you whether you were aware that he made an announcement that he was severing -- a public announcement that he was severing any cooperation with the RSK until it elected another leadership. And you actually should know that, because it's about the Vance Plan at that time, and you were very much involved at that time in Glina, were you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite honest, of course I was involved, among other reasons because Mr. Milosevic was unable to communicate with him. He asked me to go there and talk to the representative of the Krajina leadership. But to be quite honest, I don't think Mr. Milosevic knows about all the statements I made and all the letters I wrote, just as I don't know about all of his. For instance, this thing that you are quoting now, later on when I retired from politics and severed all ties with Republika Srpska because of their rejection of peace plans, I did something similar maybe, but I don't know anything about this statement that Mr. Milosevic allegedly made about severing all the ties with Serbian Krajina. I know about the Bosnian leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is this statement made? Is it a speech or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will -- when we speak about the Vance Plan a little bit later on, I will actually put it again to Mr. Kostic, because we actually do have a reference in Mr. Jovic's book about what was said, and we also have a -- an article dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but where was it said?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was actually said in Belgrade. It was not said in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was it in a meeting, in a speech, or what?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was a public announcement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But that's a meaningless expression. The witness has already said that there was an open letter written in --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It was a speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That is at least my understanding, and I will come back to it when we discuss the Vance Plan. I will go through several documents in relation to that, including this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, given Mr. Milosevic's powerful position in Serbia, within this group of six or the six men, Mr. Milosevic was the most powerful, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're not going to think that I, from Montenegro with only 600.000 population, was more influential than Mr. Milosevic who was representing 10 million people in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to quote from a -- from talks, and it's an interview that you had with Monitor, the magazine in Montenegro, but I first would like to have it distributed to everybody. Mr. Kostic, do you remember that you gave this interview or talks on the 21st of October, 1994? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's a long interview, and I don't want to actually go through all of it, just the passages that concern us at the moment.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In three instalments.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yes. First of all, at the very beginning --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in the English it's on page 3.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- you're asked about your contacts with Mr. Milosevic, and you say -- you say here: "... when I held office, I could say that we had been in contact and we communicated on a daily basis." It's in the beginning. I remember -- is that so, that you had -- while you were in the office and the Presidency that you had contacts on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say it was on a daily basis, but I can say that we communicated very frequently, because the times were very dramatic, and both he and I spent our days in our offices from dusk till dawn. We often had lunch in his office or in mine, but I never visited him at home. I never had any occasion to meet anyone from his family. But it was quite a normal communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a little bit further down, and it actually should be marked on your copy --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, it's on page 4 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- you say or, rather, it's put here: "Milosevic, who is incidentally rather distrustful, suspicious, for a long time had incomparably more trust in Bulatovic and the whole group of the young Montenegrin leadership than in me. That is how it was until The Hague." So after The Hague he had more trust in you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was not expressed in the most fortunate way. I can't say that he suddenly had more trust in me after The Hague, but as for the young Montenegrin leadership, whom I didn't know mainly before 1989, Bulatovic and others, they were aged 25 or around that, it's a rather large team. They succeeded in convincing the public of Montenegro that I was infiltrated somehow among them as an old-timer who was there to look after the interests of the old guard, and that was the image that followed me. I believe not only in the eye of -- eyes of Mr. Milosevic and the Serbian leadership, but also because the Montegnegrin leadership was viewed as separatist, and the people who were in power during the war are now the most vociferous advocates of Montenegro separating from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, but really refrain yourself to answer just the question. It was actually a simple one. A little bit further down on page 5 in the English, you are actually asked about the party of Mr. Seselj, and you say - it's on the bottom - you say --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you help me? Which instalment is that? Because there were three instalments in the Monitor magazine. Is that the first, second, or third?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think Seselj is mentioned in the second one. It's quite funny, this interview. I'd like to read it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to ask you one -- one point in that interview. I don't want to go into relationships that -- actually, when you look -- when you look at the ERN number on top, it says 0424-7290. That's -- that's --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I actually want to refer to one remark in this. It should be at the end of it. You say the following: "The question was the radicals now aggressively accuse the Montegnegrin leaders of being criminals," and so on. That's the question. And then you say: "That has nothing to do with it. I'm not denying that within my ruling party there are those who spread such rumours." And then you say: "I claim even today that Seselj and his radicals helped Milosevic a lot in his quarrel with Draskovic and Micunovic." And my question to you is does this refer to 1991 or to which period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was talking about 1991. That's the time when I was in Belgrade, and I was very well -- very knowledgeable about the situation. And as for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Draskovic and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And if you now continue a bit further down, and it's when you speak about the power in parties --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's page 6, Your Honour, in the English, the very last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Monitor magazine asked you -- and you actually have it marked, you have that passage marked on the page 0424-7290, and it's marked here. On the last column, it says: "At that time you were neglected as the head of the Montenegrin state," and it says here, your answer, that is: "That is right. Power was primarily concentrated in the party, not the institutions." Mr. Kostic, was that the same in Serbia, that the power was with the party and not so much with the institutions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that reliably about Serbia, but I know about Montenegro for the simple reason that -- and I may be partially to blame, although I don't think I made a mistake, I was simply abiding by the constitution. I was president of the Presidency of Montenegro, and according to the Montenegrin constitution, the president of the Presidency was, let me not say English Queen, but it was quite --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think you have answered the question. You said you can't say that for Serbia because you don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not clear to me, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what is meant by "the institutions." Parliamentary institutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, not only -- well, I think we have to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you said that, Mr. Kostic, when you said that is right, power was primarily concentrated in the party, not the institutions, what institutions do you mean, all the parliamentary institutions or even the ministries?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in the ruling party, which was also my party -- right now I don't belong to any party --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I -- I will have to be a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is not -- this is not a university. We don't need the introduction. Just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I said very clearly: In the party rather than the institutions. I meant the institutions of the system, but I had wanted to explain that my party then also had a two-third majority in the parliament. So what the inner circle of the party agreed as the policy, that was implemented everywhere, including institutions. I think that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So by "institutions" you mean all institutions; parliamentary and otherwise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The institutions of the system; the parliament, the government, various ministries, and that was a cause of great disappointment to me, because in all those transformations that took place at the time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was expecting to see a move towards democracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just one more quote from this series of instalments that you speak, and in the English it's on page 10, the upper answer that Mr. Kostic gives to a question; and for you, Mr. Kostic, it's on page 0424-7293 on the very top left. And Monitor asked you: "Who was in favour of peace then?" And your answer is: "It is true that both Milosevic and Bulatovic used to claim: 'Montenegro is not at war,' 'Serbia is not at war.' I never said that. I was always saying: 'Both Serbia and Montenegro were at war as well as this part of Yugoslavia.' They were, through their JNA. That army never broke up and I assert that every other army would break up in such circumstances. Mr. Mesic's departure and with the switch to operations in circumstances of imminent threat of war, as the vice-president of the country's Presidency, I practically became the head of state. I held then, as I hold today, that the greatest responsibility still lay with Milosevic as the President of Serbia, the man with the strongest influence and with the greatest pedigree of a statesman, according to his decisions and conduct." This is what you said in 1994 about responsibilities. Yes, and it's --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you awaiting a response?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you said and that's what you meant and that's what you observed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. Quite naturally. Milosevic had the greatest political authority and influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It's time for the --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Oh, just one -- I would like to tender this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I also -- I forgot to tender the Bulatovic book, the passage that I quoted from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the passage quoted will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the extract from Kostic Bulatovic's book "Rules of Silence" will be Exhibit 942, and interview given be Branko Kostic to the Monitor magazine will be Exhibit 943.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, during the examination-in-chief you spoke about the downfall of the Montenegrin government of Mr. Vukadinovic in 1988. We do not need to go into details, just this question: The protesters that actually were asking in the rallies that some of the members of the government should resign, these protesters did not really -- did not ask for your resignation; right? They asked for the resignation of others.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And unlike these other members of the government of Mr. Vukadinovic, you survived the fall of the then political leadership; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was the one from that government that continued in politics. Others continued as well, but in other political parties and other posts.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you managed to survive politically in 1988 because you shared Mr. Milosevic's views at that time and his policies and the demands that the protesters had; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As brief as possible, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Mr. Milosevic's expectations were, but I said during my examination-in-chief what I expected from those changes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the new Montegnegrin leaders, Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. Djukanovic, they also came in power in that same wave of changes that Mr. Milosevic headed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you should press him to answer that question that you asked previously, whether he survived politically because he shared Mr. Milosevic's views at that time and his policies. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think he said yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You said yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. That's at least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I need to repeat, because I think I heard him say "Da," and I didn't look to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I asked you before we spoke about Djukanovic and Bulatovic, you shared Mr. Milosevic's view or, rather, the wave of demands by the Serbs and the Montenegrins that he headed as well; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I didn't know what Mr. Milosevic's views and standpoints were at the time in their entirety because I hadn't met him since we were students. But I have already stated in my testimony so far what my expectations were. If you want a more detailed answer, I'll tell you that I don't know what contributed to my political survival at the time, but I do know that my nomination was put forward by the Republican Conference of the Socialist League of the Working People of Montenegro, which had the same composition as previously, before these events. Perhaps it was my participation in extinguishing the flames in Rozaje, Plavno, Niksic and other places in Montenegro and my successful speeches to those rallies where I managed to calm down the passions of the crowd and got the crowd to disperse probably influenced that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: To be specific, more specific, your position at that time was that Montenegro and Serbia were disadvantaged in Yugoslavia compared to other republics and that's just what also Mr. Milosevic felt; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My standpoint never referred to Serbia, because there were others taking care of Serbia. But at the time I felt that Montenegro was badly neglected in economic terms, first of all. And secondly, I supported the motives of the crowds that gathered, and I demanded that the policy of expelling Serbs and Montenegrins from Kosovo be halted. This had been taking place for decades. Also, I advocated that the Serbian people in Croatia be protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And like Mr. Milosevic, you were also dissatisfied with Mr. Markovic's measures in relation to Yugoslavia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially I even expressed public support to Mr. Ante Markovic's economic programme. However, when he, as the federal Prime Minister, was not prepared for a full year to deal with the issue of foreign exchange differences in -- differentials in Montenegro, and when he agreed to establish a political party with a rally at Kosare, I turned my back on him because of the economic problems in Montenegro and his unwillingness to deal with them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And just like Mr. Milosevic, you were -- you were in favour of the amendments to the Serbian constitution regarding Vojvodina and Kosovo. That was you agreed to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the last issue, you said during the examination-in-chief, and I refer here to transcript T-47612, you said: "The leaderships in Kosovo and Metohija on one hand and the Vojvodina on the other hand had secessionist or, rather, autonomous leanings and only a popular movement could contribute to bringing about a change in these leaderships as well." Mr. Kostic, you know that the Vojvodina authorities or populations at no time were secessionist; right? At that time there was no movement there that wanted to sever Vojvodina from Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps you know that better than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You have to answer this question. You have said it actually here. You mentioned Vojvodina in this context, and I put to you that there was no secessionist movement.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you keep asserting that. That's why I said perhaps you know that better than I do, but I don't agree with you. Don't try to put your opinions in my mouth. On the contrary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: She is putting perfectly proper questions to you, and you must answer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the population --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered that I disagreed with what the lady's saying. The leaderships both in Kosovo and Vojvodina advocated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The people in Vojvodina did not pose any threats to Serbs or Serbia, and they did not give any reason to revoke their autonomy. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are you reading this from?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not reading it. I'm putting this to you. I'm not reading it. I'm just putting this to you. Do you claim -- do you claim that the people from Vojvodina did pose a threat to Serbs or Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where you get these claims from. I mentioned the leaderships in Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija. I wasn't referring to the people but to the leaderships. It was the leaderships that were replaced through the mass rallies, not the people. I cannot tell you what you want me to say in my testimony. There was no threat to Serbia and Serbs from the people of Vojvodina, but the leaderships in both Kosovo and Metohija and Vojvodina had separatist tendencies and leanings, and the masses wanted the leaderships to be replaced.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, who -- and you speak to Vojvodina. Can you give us the names of the movements or the people that wanted to separate or secede from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, it was 15 years ago, and to give you a list of names, it would be very hard to do that even in the case of Montenegro let alone Vojvodina. And I come from Montenegro. But I do remember vividly that individuals from the leaderships of Vojvodina and from Kosovo and Metohija were more willing to support the standpoints of the Slovenians or the Croats than their own republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Following the ousting of the Vojvodina government in the course of 1989 and 1990, the autonomous status of Kosovo and Vojvodina were removed. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's not correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Only those provisions whereby the autonomous provinces had been given the right to pass legislation without the approval of the Assembly of Serbia, but the Assembly of Serbia could pass no legislation without the approval of the autonomous provinces. It was this provision that was abolished. I felt that this put Serbia into an unequal footing as compared to all the other Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, a few moments ago we had discussed that the Serbian Assembly actually replaced the member in the Federal Presidency from Kosovo. So there was quite a different change there, isn't it? Based on the changes in 1998 and 1990, the Serbian Assembly could simply replace the member of the Kosovo -- the representative of Kosovo and Metohija in the Federal Presidency. So the change was quite a different one than you say.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I mentioned this during my testimony, but the constitution of 1974 included many confederal elements, and the autonomous provinces were even given a constituent character within the Yugoslav federation. I'm not aware of the details concerning the changes in the constitution of Serbia, but I assert with confidence that the autonomy of neither of these provinces was abolished but certain provisions were abolished which put Serbia in -- onto an unequal footing with other republics because of the confederal nature of those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you just said that the Yugoslav constitution of 1974 for Vojvodina and Kosovo and Metohija, both were constituent elements of that federation, and the autonomous provinces had a representative in the SFRY Presidency and they had their own delegations in both Chambers in the federal parliament. That's correct; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Therefore, the changes in the constitutional status of the autonomous provinces immediately impacted on the balance of power in the federal -- on the federal level, isn't it?
