utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because in spite of the changes introduced by Serbia into its constitution, the provinces continued to be represented in the Yugoslav Presidency and the Yugoslav parliament. They retained their representatives in the parliament.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I have probably formulated too vaguely, but what we have seen is that the Serbian Assembly, according to the changes that were made in 1990, could elect certainly the member of the Presidency for Kosovo and Metohija, and they could do the same and did the same for Vojvodina. So how can that not be a power change? If the Serbian Assembly can basically decide who represents Kosovo and Metohija and who represents Vojvodina, that's definitely a much more powerful position than the Croats had, the Slovenes, the Macedonians, or the Bosnians. You would agree to that? You must, actually.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But, madam, it was not changes in government. It was changes in competency. Changes in competency occurred, because some issues that were within the purview of the autonomous provinces, according to the previous constitution, were transferred to the republic, but the autonomous provinces continued. And I can tell you that were you at the head of a state or a territory, you as the person responsible for the entire territory of that state would certainly take care to influence what was happening there. But Serbia, until those changes, did not have the power to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We heard, actually -- Mr. Kostic, we heard quite some evidence on this point from the historian Ms. Budding, from Petar Kriste - Your Honour, that's at T-14891 - by Nikola Samardzic, that is T-11165; Milan Kucan, and I do not want to quote them here, but I just want to refer you to the person that you actually have mentioned as being a reliable one, and that is Aleksandar Vasiljevic. He was also talking of -- about this situation, and he actually said the following -- and, Your Honours, it's at transcript 15859 to 60. This is what he said about this: "Real power at that time resided in the republican leaders, while the members of the Presidency were, if I can express myself metaphorically, ambassadors representing their own republics and provinces in the Presidency." And a little bit further down: "I don't think he -" and he refers here to Mr. Milosevic - "his position was any different than that of the presidents of the other republics, but there is no doubt that he was a very strong political leader, that he was very authoritative and that because of this he was in reality able to influence four of the members of the Presidency." And he is referring then to these four members. I just wanted to remind you to what Mr. Vasiljevic said on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's the question you're putting in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to -- my question to you is that Mr. Milosevic, or the Serbian leadership, rather, controlled the votes of four members of the SFRY Presidency.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I have to correct you. In my previous testimony, I did not say that Mr. Vasiljevic was a reliable witness, because I don't want to take it upon myself to evaluate the character of any individual, including Mr. Vasiljevic. I only said on one occasion that what Mr. Vasiljevic said concerning some communications and so on and so forth would probably know about that better than I do, in view of his position. As to what you have just asked me now, I think there is no doubt that at the time when I was part of the Presidency of the SFRY the presidents of the republics had taken it upon themselves to try and find solutions to the Yugoslav crisis. And if I had any objection to the work of Mr. Milosevic or Mr. Bulatovic, it was precisely that they had taken on this role. Your claim that Mr. Milosevic exerted a direct influence or control over me is completely incorrect. I am a mature, grown-up person, and I made decisions based on my own thoughts. And as I have already said, there were many issues on which Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Jovic, and I did not agree and took different standpoints. But I have said that, yes, Mr. Milosevic was an influential person with a lot of political authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, to go back to this table that was produced according to the book of Mr. Jovic, you can see easily when comparing the columns where Mr. Milosevic is mentioned and Mr. Kadijevic and Mr. Jovic are mentioned. If you look at these columns, you can easily see that although Mr. Milosevic was not a member of the SFRY Presidency, he and Mr. Jovic met with the military more often than you did in the period that we are concerned with. You can see that it's obvious, in particular, from the first page. You can easily see that and it continues to be like this until the end of October 1991. That means, at least as I read it, that he de facto as the President of Serbia was much more important for the JNA leadership than you, despite your position. That's what I read from this chart. Would you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is based on a misrepresentation that these are sessions of the Presidency of the SFRY. These are not sessions of the Presidency. This has been constructed from various notes in the book, and it puts together various meetings of a diverse nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say, and it doesn't say on this sheet that it was meetings between -- it's meetings. I have already mentioned it, and Judge Bonomy has corrected it as well. The headline can be ignored. What I said when we spoke about this sheet is that it's referring to meetings within the Presidency and outside the Presidency. That's what I have already corrected, with the help of Judge Bonomy who noticed that the headline is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by "within the Presidency"? You put a footnote that this overview does not include Presidency sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I must admit at the moment I'm at a loss what this means. My understanding is it is the meetings between members of the Rump Presidency and the military and these other people belonging to the group of six, no matter where they took place. That's at least my understanding of the situation. It's the meetings of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So meetings of one party. The group of six on the one end --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the meetings of the group of six, including the military. That's what I refer here to in this sheet. The members of the Office of the Prosecutor went through the book of Mr. Jovic and has actually -- have actually listed who -- who met in that period we are concerned with and in particular Mr. Kostic is concerned with. It's just the period that Mr. Kostic is actually involved here. And we have noted from all his entries in the book when they met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, in earlier session you clarified in a question to the Presiding Judge that it means the meeting of the group of six people, on the one hand, and military on the other hand. So could you check it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The point I'm actually making, Mr. Kostic, and my question to you was that although Mr. Milosevic was not a member of the Presidency, he and Mr. Jovic met with the military outside of the Presidency, meeting, of course, more often than you did in that period. And my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let him --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: According to that sheet, it actually looks like it, and you just see it's very obvious --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you cannot allow such nonsense. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff herself said that this is exacted from Jovic's book based on his notes. Her question sounds as if she had a document showing when the witness met with the military leadership. Even Jovic in his book does not deal with Kostic's meetings, and I think that this is not even correct. If it's from the book, it's not correct. There couldn't have been six meetings in May, six or seven in June. Nobody would have been doing anything else then. It's impossible. Whether they met, that's a different issue. But there's nothing about meetings between the witness and the military leadership that can be compared to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind -- never mind the source. What's to prevent her from putting that you met with the military leadership more than this witness. Never mind the source. I think the question can be put and it's for the witness to say yes or no. Just put the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, did -- according to that sheet here, according to Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Never mind the sheet. Never mind the sheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. According to the book of Mr. Jovic, it seems that he and Milosevic met the military leadership more often than you did. Is that the correct view or not? Did they meet more often with Milosevic and Jovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief, I said quite decidedly I did not keep tabs on this. Who Mr. Jovic or who Mr. Milosevic were meeting, that's something I can't say, especially on the basis of this information that you say comes from Jovic's book. During the examination-in-chief, I said, I said that some information from Jovic's book should be taken with reservations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The witness says he's not in a position to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to be correct and be specific about the sheet -- the table, the remark here on the bottom, "This overview does not include regular Presidency sessions," that's correct. It includes only meetings out of -- outside the former framework of the Presidency. So the footnote was correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In -- we will go into quite some details a little bit later on on political conflicts that Mr. Milosevic had with the Montenegrin president, Mr. Bulatovic. When those conflicts arose - and I refer here in particular to the Carrington Plan, the withdrawal of Montenegrin soldiers from the front lines in Croatia and others that I will speak to you about - you usually would take Mr. Milosevic's point of view and not support Bulatovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not support Milosevic by that, but I assessed at the time, and I think that later developments prove me right, that in that period, that is say from October 1991 onwards, the immediate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- state leadership --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- you can answer that question more directly than you are doing. The question is relatively simple, and it is whether in relation to the conflicts, in particular the Carrington Plan, the withdrawal of Montenegrin soldiers from the front lines in Croatia, that generally you supported Mr. Milosevic's point of view as distinct from the position of Mr. Bulatovic. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite simply I don't want to answer a question put that way. All I want to say with respect to The Hague document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's not for you to determine whether the question is permissible. That's for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I can answer specifically. As far as The Hague document is concerned, Mr. Milosevic and I had the same position, as opposed to Mr. Bulatovic with respect to the withdrawal of part of the army from Montenegro, from Banija, and I state that quite clearly in my book, and I'm sure the Prosecution has that portion. Mr. Bulatovic, as president of the Presidency of Montenegro, called me in Podgorica to attend a meeting of the Presidency of Montenegro, and they offered that I sign a request for fighters to return from Banija. I refused to do that categorically and told them that even if I didn't think the opposite, I couldn't do that because it wasn't part of my purview as vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, that it was up to the General Staff or, rather, the Staff of the Supreme Command, and I also told him that pursuant to the constitution it was even less up to him to sign this request that the fighters return from the front, because this came under the purview of federal organs and federal institutions, and I think that's a complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In February 1992, there was a dispute between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bulatovic regarding the command of the new army of the new Yugoslavia, put it that simple. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you must be more specific, what you have in mind. Do you mean when the constitutional foundations for the new Yugoslavia were established?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, but I think it's easier -- I will put to you from the book "Rules of Silence" of Mr. Bulatovic, I will put a quote to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And can this please be provided to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And as you say, it's indeed about the new Yugoslavia that you discussed in February and also even starting in January 1992 and who would command the army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the constitutional foundations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And I would like to quote to you from page 2. And you have only one page, and it's here actually indicated with a frame on your page. "From your perspective, the things stood as follows: Branko Kostic --" "From our perspective, the things stood as follows: Branko Kostic had much more understanding for Slobodan Milosevic's proposal than he had for my counter-arguments, and he justified that with federal functions." And I drop now a part that's not so relevant. "During the discussion about the Supreme Defence Council and the command over the Yugoslav army, Milosevic and I could not -- could in no way find a solution. He requested that the president of the state be given the command, and I wanted it to be a collective decision of all three members of the Council; that is, the presidents of the republics and that it be established by consensus." And now I drop also a little part, and then it continues: "As far as I was concerned, we could have done it for 44 hours, for I did not want to give in because of a recent experience of life importance. I did not want any president of Montenegro or Serbia to experience in the future the things I had experienced when helplessly watching soldiers from Montenegro being sent to Banija. Responsibility for their lives was objectively my due, and my influence on that decision was equal to zero. I deemed necessary that these two things be coordinated, and that responsibility not be valid only after the fact, but also prior to the decision being reached." And he also refers then to, let's say, a little bit of forth and back about formulations. Do you recall that; and if so, is it true that you took Mr. Milosevic's view?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you formulated the question properly. I did not join in Mr. Milosevic's views, but in that discussion I demonstrated profound disagreement with the position expressed by Mr. Momir Bulatovic. Now, these discrepancies between us began earlier, because what Mr. Momir Bulatovic advocated at the time when he says that he debated it for four hours, he was in fact advocating in that new Yugoslavia once again some sort of confederal element and some sort of collective leadership, collective management of the army, with a general consensus and so on and so forth. Now, I came out in favour of another option that the new Federal Republic of Yugoslavia should be a modern, functional federation, and that's where we didn't see eye-to-eye and clashed in our party organs. I was still in the party then, and Mr. Bulatovic was president of the party. So our views clashed there and at the Assembly. In the Montenegrin Assembly I came out publicly in defending the position that Montenegro could not in that new Yugoslavia insist on having 50 per cent of the share in the Yugoslav People's Army. And if that were the case, then it would have to accept 50 per cent of the costs, and 50 per cent of the diplomats in the diplomatic service, and then it would have to cover 50 per cent of the costs and expenditure for those services. I assumed that in establishing these constitutional foundations - and that's what we're talking about, madam, the constitutional foundations - we should not be allowed in Montenegro to take a position or to take any rigid, rigorous positions which could later on lead Serbia not to accept those principles for a common state.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I have to say -- may I just be allowed to say one more sentence? I have to say that in that connection there were serious manipulations in the leadership of my won party at the Main Board of the Democratic Party of Socialists. We discussed this at much greater length, but Mr. Bulatovic doesn't write about any of that in this book of his. So in order to --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- marry the two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I ask, what was your view about how the army should be commanded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My view was that the command of the army in that state should belong not to the presidents of the republics but to the institution at the level of the federal state. Mr. Bonomy, I considered that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How did that differ from Mr. Milosevic's view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't say that it was opposed to his view, but I didn't join in Milosevic's view but defended this as my own view. But I strongly stood up against the position expressed by Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But, you see, that is a very unhelpful way of approaching virtually every question that you're asked, because it seems to me that the actual answer to the question is that you and Mr. Milosevic agreed, and disagreed with Mr. Bulatovic. Simple answer. And if I've got that wrong, if I've got that basic position wrong, please correct me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think you have got it wrong. First, I'm not a child to join in anybody else's opinion. I am somebody with my own integrity and I have my own position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is such a childish attitude. Everything has to come from your perspective: Me, me, me. Why can't you just think about the question you're being asked and answer it in a straightforward way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, what Mr. Milosevic's -- what Mr. Milosevic accepted during our joint discussions I would never have accepted. I would have stood firm on the position that that new state should be a modern, functional federation and that under its competency and purview and power it has four or five basic functions; that it have defence under its remit, that it has customs policies, the monetary system, and so on, and at the level of that federal state to have its own institutions through which it would realise those powers of it. Now, Mr. Milosevic accepted something I would never have accepted, in the quest for a compromise solution, probably, or for reaching an agreement; I don't know that. He'll be best placed to answer that himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender the -- this section of Bulatovic's book as part of Exhibit 942.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about keeping the same number as the one we have already admitted. So all as parts of Mr. Bulatovic's book "Rules of Silence."

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's the proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to complete this, the question that was asked some time ago was: "In February 1992 there was a dispute between Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bulatovic regarding the command of the new army of the new Yugoslavia, put it that simple." So that, Mr. Kostic, was the issue, not the overall general structure of the institutions of the new state. Please carry on, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to explain, Mr. Bonomy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. The Prosecutor will ask you what questions she wishes and Mr. Milosevic can re-examine on it if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you in the Presidency, in the Federal Presidency, was the one to represent the Montenegrin interest in -- on the federal level, but you do not support your own president, Mr. Bulatovic, on this important issue where it really goes to the heart of the influence that the Montenegrin leadership can have on this federal level. That's -- don't you think that's strange that you do not represent the Montenegrin interest?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely through my desire to represent the interests of Montenegro to the end that I firmly adhere to the position I expounded a moment ago, because I consider and I think that time did tell that the confederal elements as a collective command, a collective leadership and so on and so forth, do not give the prospects of that common state having a life. And from the very first day I did everything in my power to retain and preserve that state. A compromise solution was found and then it was said in the constitutional groundworks they refer -- what was referred to was a united armed forces and united command; however, the leadership of Montenegro - that is to say my colleagues from the top political echelons of Montenegro - manipulated the matter at the time as well, and instead of expanding on -- and saying "united," they put "joint."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... here. Now let me interrupt you here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've asked me a question and not given me the opportunity of answering it. Mr. Robinson --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the answer, and it didn't really go to the issue.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you didn't let me finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, in 1990 -- in the spring of 1992, it was agreed that the first president of the new Yugoslavia should be nominated by Montenegro. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the -- your party, the Democratic Party of Socialists nominated Mr. Svetozar Marovic. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's your party. They want him in this position.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: However, you also then can -- became a candidate, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's put it this way: You were asked to -- for candidature on this point. You were asked.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Who asked you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, five minutes before the Federal Assembly went into session, it was Mr. Seselj that asked for a meeting and told me that his rather numerous group of deputies in the parliament would like to put forward my name as candidate. And I said that my party had proposed a candidate already on behalf of the Democratic Party of Socialists of Montenegro, and that I couldn't accept it without having consulted my party first. We held those consultations, and my party did not lend its support but went through with its original proposal and I did not accept myself being put forward as a candidate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic proposed that you should -- should have a candidature for the Presidency, for the president of the new Yugoslavia. Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the first time I've heard of it. I think that I found somewhere -- I do apologise, but I think there's somewhere in Boro Jovic's book I did find a passage -- or once again from his notes, an assertion to the effect that he and Milosevic talked to me. Mr. Milosevic just in one talk offered me the post of defence minister, and I said to him on that occasion if Mr. Bulatovic as president of Montenegro and president of the ruling party in Montenegro, and you Mr. Milosevic as President of Serbia and president of the ruling party in Serbia take it upon yourselves, the two most important posts in that new state, that in that case I would be prepared to continue my political engagement and take up political functions. As that did not happen, I thanked them and returned to the university because I considered that at the outset it was the two most prominent figures should assume those two most prominent posts, functions in the federal state, all the more so as all the international deputies and representatives had communicated with them previously as presidents of the republics.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me quote from Exhibit 596, tab 3. It's Mr. Jovic's book on Milosevic and I refer to the pages 87 and 88. Yes. We can put this on the ELMO, but I have actually -- I quote first from page -- quote 87, 88: "It is obvious --" and it's about -- in this relation he speaks first about Mr. Marovic not being known to -- on the federal level and to Mr. Milosevic, and it says here: "It is obvious that it influenced Milosevic, who was pulling all strings and making personnel and other decisions in that transitive situation, to try to impose his own candidate for Montenegro, one that he could trust. Milosevic wanted Branko Kostic ... nominate himself for the FRY president ... He was extremely cooperative and loyal in the period of the efforts for preserving Yugoslavia and the defence of the Serbian people's interest. In the critical moments, he was even more on the side of Serbian than the Montenegrin interests" Then a little bit further down: "Slobodan's idea is that Branko Kostic found certain support in Montenegro, if he is not able in his party then out of it, and we will elect him regardless of the will of the Montenegro Democratic Party of Socialists. He says he already got consent for he --" that's Mr. Milosevic. "He says he already got consent from Vojislav Seselj and he believes that the other parties will prefer to vote for Branko Kostic than for Marovic. He suggests that I organise a meeting with Branko Kostic and persuade him to accept that proposal of his." And you agreed to this proposal, did you not, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that what you've just read out is what it says there, but none of it is correct. None of what Mr. Borisav Jovic says is correct. And I've already said that you should take some of his assertions with reservations. Nor did he write that as a diary. In that book of his he says that on the 14th of July we made the decision to withdraw the army from Slovenia, whereas we did that on the 18th of July. So what Mr. Jovic says here is incorrect. And there are many other things that are not correct in books that I've read on subjects that I've talked about, and it's also incorrect that I ever proclaimed that I would put myself forth as a candidate, and Mr. Jovic goes on in the text to discuss my fate and my destiny and an attitude towards me linked to Dobrica Cosic's orientation, and so on. The full truth is that we had three consultations about cadre solutions for the post of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. At two of these consultations nobody except for me made any mention of a single name, and at the first and at the second and at the third meeting I persisted in repeating that the two most responsible posts in the federal state must be taken over by the two most prominent men, that is to say Mr. Milosevic and Momir Bulatovic, without entering in who will be Prime Minister and who would be president of the state, of the country. So those strivings of mine --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you here. Mr. Jovic wouldn't have any reason to make something like this up, would he? There is no reason for him to just make this up.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, let me tell you, Mr. Bulatovic in his book said that we drank coffee at Batajnica airport before we took off in the plane. Quite incorrect. So this is incorrect too. I can't say anything else but that it is incorrect, not true. I have no other choice. And I can also add that we were the last people at the -- or, rather, that Mr. Bulatovic be proposed as candidate and that that had been already decided in the party leadership.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, before you ask the witness whether he agreed to the suggestion of Milosevic and Jovic, why don't you put the passage where he described a meeting in a villa in Dedinje. It's the last paragraph of 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "We met in a villa in Dedinje where Branko Kostic lived. Slobodan was avoiding starting the conversation because certain master of the house was bustling around and serving coffee and other drinks and he felt unpleasant to ask him to leave. All three of us went out and started the conversation in the garden. Slobodan was explaining to Branko the whole idea and the ways of implementing. "Branko agreed. He was convinced that this move was good for the future of Yugoslavia because he was, similarly like us, very critical about the behaviour of Montenegrin leadership in the period of Yugoslav partition." He is very precise about what is actually discussed and where. And actually, I think I even continue here: "Soon he announced -" he, that's you - "announced that he would run for office, and this caused even more considerable distrust and suspicion among the republic leadership and especially a storm of resistance in the official Montenegro leadership." So he's very precise.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very convincing, I have to say. Perhaps that's something Mr. Jovic dreamt of. But the description is very convincing, and it's almost -- it's very difficult for one not to believe it, but all I can say is that this whole story about the running for office and all this time that nothing was known was just two days; it was the weekend. And Mr. Seselj, when prior to the Assembly session suggested that his party, his deputies would put me forward as candidate and I said that I would consult my own party, that is why the election was put off for two days. I think it was left to Monday or the following week, the Wednesday. So there couldn't have been much discussion or dilemma on that point. And ultimately, why would I accept it in that conversation of running for office? It was highly unreasonable, Mr. Seselj putting me forward, bypassing the support from my party and my party's supporters, and why Mr. Milosevic and Jovic wouldn't have put my name forward themselves as candidate.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, did Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Jovic visit your villa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in two villas. I mostly lived in Uzicka Street number 16, and for the last month I lived in what was known as the Vojvodina villa. And as far as I know, as far as I remember, Milosevic and Jovic never visited me in that villa. I really don't remember them ever having come there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic did visit me once. I don't know whether it was April or May. He visited me in this villa, and that was the only villa, the villa in Uzicka number 16. But the villa was supposed to be adapted, reconstructed, whatever. So there was discussion over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't need all these details, Mr. Kostic. I knew it wouldn't be simple. There's bound to be more than one villa for a start. The villa in Dedinje is the one referred to in the question. Now, which of the villas is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was official accommodation, Mr. Bonomy, both of them. Mr. Bonomy, it was official accommodation. I had an apartment, one apartment in one of those villas. For a time I was in one, for a time I was in another, when I moved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In that one that is referred to in that book, did Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Jovic visit you there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said no. No. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is it "no" or is it "I can't remember"? Which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what benefit would Mr. Jovic have to make up such a lie?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's something you would have to ask him. I really can't answer that question. Why would he do that? Why can you find very bad lies in some other books? You can ask that question as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found Mr. Mesic in his book telling so many untruthful things already.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You are evading, actually, to answer. I asked you what benefit would there be in for Mr. Jovic and your answer would actually have to be "There is no benefit in making up this lie."

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, he's answered the question: "Ask Mr. Jovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: He hasn't answered the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I want to quote still from the book how this concluded, and it's on page 89 at the bottom and the following page: "Slobodan Milosevic called me to inform me about the definite proposal of the FRY president, just like nothing has happened, like we had not talked with Branko Kostic. He told me that we would go for Dobrica Cosic, that we wouldn't nominate him or probably that we would vote for him. He said he had talked with Dobrica and that he had agreed." And, Mr. Kostic, that was the reason why you withdrew your nomination for president; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not how it was, ma'am. That's your conclusion. Please don't expect me to confirm your conclusion. I'm saying this is a fabrication. It's made up. There are many things that are made up, in that book and in many others you've quoted from.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the beginning of your testimony, you said that in June 1992, you withdrew from political life. Mr. Kostic, you were expelled from your own party; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: End 1992. But in mid-1992, I withdrew from political life, because it was my personal decision. And in end 1992, the leadership of my party expelled me from the party.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your remark that you withdrew from political life is not entirely true, because you campaigned against Momir Bulatovic for the president position in Montenegro in December 1992, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, on the 15th of June, I stopped being vice-president of the Presidency of the SFRY, and by December I had withdrawn from political life completely. In December, there were presidential elections in Montenegro, and one of the presidential candidates was Momir Bulatovic, as nominated by the ruling Socialist Party --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and there were another seven or eight people running for that office. And there was also a group of citizens --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why can't you just say whether or not you campaigned for the office of president against Mr. Bulatovic? It's a simple question. It's either yes or it's no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Mr. Bonomy, but five or six months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- after I withdrew from my political life. And if I can explain very briefly why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. No explanation, please. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: During the campaign in December 1992 in Montenegro, the Montenegrin leadership strived for more independence from Serbia, did it? And you did not approve of this; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic supported you in your campaign; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put again a quote from Mr. Bulatovic's book "Rules of Silence" to you. And it will be given to everybody here because we would like to tender this afterwards into evidence. We can also put it on the ELMO. We can put it on the ELMO and provide the copies later. Mr. Kostic, it's a meeting that Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Bulatovic have after the election, obviously, and Mr. Bulatovic said the following: "I heard him out and, regaining my composure, shook his hand and said: 'This is the hand of real cooperation between the presidents of Montenegro and Serbia. I know that your candidate was Branko Kostic. His Belgrade election headquarters was in your cabinet. Your man of confidence, Mihalj Kertes, brought information over on a special flight, which was supposed to compromise me in a TV debate ...'" And then he continues and says: "Then the phone rang --" Let's say -- I'd rather read the whole thing. "He wouldn't give in. He defended himself with a torrent of words. It is impossible that I would buy into such disinformation. My information is wrong and my sources malevolent. He would never even think of doing something like that, and the like. Then the phone rang. It was his wife who, when she found out I was there, wanted to congratulate me personally on the election. In the third sentence, she said that she kept telling Slobodan not to support Branko Kostic, but he wouldn't listen to her." This is what Mr. Bulatovic writes in his book, and he is what -- what -- he is telling the truth, does he not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not the truth, Mr. Robinson. What the lady just read from Momir Bulatovic's book was written in a book in which Bulatovic claims that I was a candidate of the Serbian Radical Party, that is not true; that the Assembly of Montenegro accepted The Hague document, which is not true; that the leadership of our common party accepted The Hague document, which is not true; that we drank coffee together in Batajnica, which again is not true. There are many things that are not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I was asking you about this very specific event and there was no need to go into other details of the book, just this one, and I understand your answer to say it's not true.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He talked to Mr. Milosevic. Mr. Milosevic can say whether that conversation took place or not. I'm just telling you that you are referring to a source which contains a lot of incorrect and untruthful things, and these are not details to me. I wrote, by the way, a very extensive critique of that book, and all these things are verifiable, based on original documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this page admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what we're considering is that consistency with our past practice would require that we don't admit it because the witness hasn't agreed or accepted your propositions, but Mr. Milosevic may have no objection to it. Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course it's pointless to exhibit books written by somebody else concerning events involving Kostic that Kostic denies. What does this prove? It proves that that man really wrote this. And I think it's really nonsense what is written. I don't want to go into the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that's probably a fair point consistently with what we've decided. The difference here, significant difference here is that the person who wrote the book is to be a witness, and therefore the position, I suppose, might change.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will not admit it now, then. Well, we can mark it for identification pending the testimony of Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour, before the break, I have to -- I've forgotten to ask admittance of one of the pages of the book of Mr. Kostic himself. It's the pages 267 to 270. We had discussed this, but I had forgotten to ask that it be admitted under tab 3 -- under --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the one page that was marked for identification will be 944 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In -- in the examination-in-chief, you had addressed with Mr. Milosevic Exhibits D333, tab 1. That's the visit of the president or ambassador of -- meeting with Dr. Nathan Shamuyarira. And I would like to speak about a few other passages in this exhibit. First, I would like to direct you to page 4 in the English, and it's how you characterised the people you were negotiating with and supposed to find peace agreements with in 1991, and you say: "I have to say that unfortunately at the beginning of this century and in the first half of the century the policies of the Catholic church and the Vatican coincided and connected rather successfully with Hitler's Nazi ideology and that we were going about the same business." That means you compared the new government of Croatia with the Hitler regime that prevailed at that time in Croatia. And you also said: "When Tudjman came to power in Croatia, that Second World War ideology began to reassert itself. Tudjman opened the borders to Ustasha who had emigrated, who had fled after the Second World War." Mr. Kostic, speaking about the people you need to discuss with and find solution with in this form wouldn't really yield any agreements. Don't you think so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's your conclusion. That didn't -- it didn't lead to a solution. That's why we were not able to find a common language or reach an agreement. And it's indisputable that even Mr. Mesic in a passage that we quoted here, as an opposition leader, when he parted ways with Tudjman, he said clearly and loudly that lots of the things that were happening in Croatia at the time recalled the times of the Independent State of Croatia. And it's also well known that the Catholic church played a very important role through the so-called rat channels in the removal of --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we're not talking now about the World War II and what happened there. I was just putting to you that if you think of your -- people you have to negotiate with, if you speak about them in this way, how could you ever think of achieving an agreement with them and a peaceful solution if you say about them they are basically representing the old Nazi regime?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, if we had been expecting a positive outcome from our talks, we wouldn't have involved the international community - primarily Europe - in those talks. You cannot disregard that. If those people were not like I said, Mr. Mesic himself would not renounce them later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when you compared the authorities in Croatia with the -- the state that actually existed, the Croatian state that existed in -- in the 1940s, you actually imply, and I think you actually said it publicly, that the Serbs in Croatia were supposed to suffer another genocide. They were threatened with another genocide. You said those things, right, at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Losing the formal status of a constituent nation does not endanger the Serbs in their survival; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand the question. Would you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When speaking about the genocide, it's often referred to the fact that the Serb people were losing the formal status of a constituent nation, and my question was to you losing this formal status of a constituent nation does not endanger the Serbs in their survival; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have endangered them, that's true. The loss of the status of constituent people for Serbs in the new Croatian constitution that establishes a nation state of Croats and relegates Serbs to a status of minority, together with all the other things that were present on the Croatian political scene at that time did present a danger, and the Serb people - and you quoted some data yourself - has become a minority in real terms in Croatia, with a share of only 4 per cent in the total population.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, actually the Serbs are listed in the preamble of the constitution of Croatia as minority, along with the assurances of proper minority rights. You know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And being a constituent nation would not have solved the problems of the Serbs living in Croatia, would it? The problems that the Serbs faced on these territories that later became the RSK, they wouldn't have been solved had they been named constituent nation in the Croatian constitution. That was not really the problem, was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, preserving the role of constituent people in Croatia from the Serbs' point of view would not have resolved their problems but would have been a much better guarantee of safety in view of their historical experience and all the things they had gone through in the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, these exaggerations surrounding this formal status was just used as a pretext for the propaganda that the Serbs were threatened with genocide. Isn't that what really was going on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your opinion, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Given your discussion with Judge Kwon on the difference in the right of a constituent nation and a minority, you said that the difference would be that on all matters of fate and destiny the decision must be taken with acquiescence of all constituent nations and that there would be no out-voting. Did I understand you correctly there in this point?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember that exchange with Mr. Kwon correctly, it had to do with the Belgrade Initiative and the constitutional arrangements that meant that all nations and all republics were included on a basis of absolute equality and without any out-voting. There was another exchange - I don't know whether it was with Mr. Kwon - concerning the constituent nature of peoples in Bosnia-Herzegovina where the constitution states that two nations cannot decide against the third one in matters of life and death, in crucial matters. There were no such provisions in the Croatian constitution requiring complete consensus on crucial, vital issues, but the constituent role for the people -- for Serb people in Croatia would have given greater guarantees to Serbs in terms of safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I had actually -- the Prosecution team looked at both the constitution of Croatia and also the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina before the amendments, and first of all, in neither of these constitutions the term "constituent peoples" is used at all. Those constitutions were not ethnically based republics. The emphasis was on the power of the working people; workers, citizens, and nations. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you that I was not a lawyer. I'm an economist, and I cannot comment on the constitutions of any of these republics, including mine. But I don't know whether it is stipulated in some part of the constitution or not, but in the rules of procedure of various bodies it was very clearly stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kostic, I also had checked the constitutions of both Croatia and Herzegovina to find out whether there is this difference between a constituent nation and a minority that you actually claimed here in your discussion with Judge Kwon; that is, that all matters of fate and destiny would have to have the consent of all constituent nations. And actually, there is no such provision, not in the Croatian constitution nor in the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you mentioned constituent or constitution forming people, whereas I talked of constituent. Maybe there is no distinction. I'm not sure. Maybe it's the same thing. But I'm telling you what I know about this matter, and I'm not an expert. If I'm mistaken somewhere, please don't take it against me, but I still believe that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the method of decision-making as far as vital decisions are concerned was stipulated in such a way that the agreement of all three constituent nations was required. Once decisions started being taken by out-voting, that started a whole process that began with the walkout of Serb representatives, the decision-making in the Bosnian parliament without Serb representation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, we don't have a translation of both the constitutions, and they are not tendered in evidence yet. The only proposal I could actually make at the moment is say that it is not in there according to our checking, and my proposal would be that we give it to -- perhaps give the B/C/S version of both constitutions to Mr. Kostic so that he can look into it over the weekend, and if he finds what he claims in there, he could then direct us to it. I mean, otherwise, it's very difficult to prove a negative when you don't have the full text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask you to intervene so that I get those copies of the constitutions of Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, because I may need them for my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is what I was going to suggest; that they be handed to the -- to Mr. Milosevic so that he may use them in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And actually, what I -- what I said to you, Mr. Kostic, about what you said to Mr. Kwon, it's in the 2nd February session where it actually is said this way as I have quoted it, just as the reference for everyone to check. I would like now to return to the Defence exhibit, tab 1. And, Mr. Kostic, I would like to direct you to page 8 in the English. And you speak with Mr. Shamuyarira about the Muslims, and you say the following, and it's on page 8: "The vast majority of the Muslims in 95 or 98 per cent of cases are Islamised Serbs, Serbs who accepted Islam, that is. However, 30 years ago, the Yugoslav authorities gave the Muslims the status of a people, a nation. This is the only example in the world of a population, a group, having its right to nationhood recognised on a purely religious basis." These Islamised Serbs, this term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's page 15 in Serbian, if I may assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us wait in the witness finds it, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This term "Islamised Serbs" for Muslims that is actually a term we have heard from Mr. Seselj here as well, but how come you used that term? Do you share his views on that, Mr. Seselj's views?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On many issues Mr. Seselj and I have completely diverging views. However, there are certain terms in the Serbian language for which there is no other word. These were indeed Serbs who used to be Orthodox Christians and who for various reasons, either for reasons of blood vendetta or for better expectations in life, converted to Islam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you or do you not share Mr. Seselj's views on this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what Mr. Seselj's view is on the matter, but I've already said here. The lady quoted the word "people." It's not the people, it's the nation. I've always said that the Yugoslav Communist Party, at one point in relation to that Yugoslav nation who was part of the population, the Yugoslav Communist Party decided they should have the status of nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: A little further on, you say: "The big problem is that in Bosnia the Serbs and the Muslims are mixed together. In 105 of 110 municipalities they live together mixed together. In some municipalities the Muslims are the ethnic majority, in some municipalities the Serbs are the ethnic majority. The Croats are ethnically fairly homogenous in Bosnia and Herzegovina. They make up about 95 per cent of the population in Western Herzegovina ..." You said that to the ambassador and that was how it was; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'd like to quote now from the next page, it's page 9, Your Honours, and -- page 9 in the English. It should be on your page or the next one. It says here: "The European Community and Mr. Badinter as president of the Arbitration Commission unfortunately suggested that a referendum be carried out among the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This means applying the principle of predominance and destroying the principle of equal right of all ... peoples in line with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is in force." Can you please explain to me how a referendum, which is actually a tool of a democratic regime, can be explained to be the principle of predominance? How can you call a democratic referendum that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, during my previous testimony I said Mr. Alija Izetbegovic had said that all that was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina was going on about 30 years too early, because in about 30 years Muslims would have an absolute majority in the population. In the then conditions of great tension in Bosnia, the only real solution was to conduct a referendum within each of the constituent peoples in Bosnia. And if all the three respective majorities were in favour of forming an independent state, then that decision would have been justified. This way, if representatives of the Serb people -- rather, not representatives but all the Serbs boycotted that referendum, held their referendum instead and the greatest majority of them voted for staying in the existing common state together with Bosnia, maybe even sovereign, but constituted along principles that would again prevent out-voting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... interrupt you here. You -- I just quoted to you that you yourself say the Serbs and the Muslims are completely mixed in 105 of these municipalities. How can a referendum for just groups of these -- for this ethnic group lead to any solution? Why not a referendum for all of them as they live all together on that same territory? I would just like you to explain to me, how would three referendums solve that situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can understand, madam, that it's truly difficult for you to comprehend this. It only goes to show how little you are familiar with the situation on the Balkans. I don't hold it against you, really, because it's impossible for you to understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's impossible for you to -- but I don't want to argue with the witness. Thank you. I will continue -- perhaps you can explain it to me and in particular to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you insist, I'll try. You see, Muslims, Croats, and Serbs, but mostly the Muslims and Serbs, were all mixed up in 105 municipalities. Muslims and Serbs in practically every municipality. These Muslims and these Serbs had their constitutional status within the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. At one point in time what happened was that the vast majority of the Muslim population at the first multi-party parliamentary elections voted for the Party of Democratic Action, which was their national and religious party, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... here. The question is very simple: How would three separate referenda solve the situation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my deep conviction, much better and in a much more peaceful way than the way it was actually solved. It was actually done on the basis of a referendum of only the Muslim and Croatian peoples in Bosnia, because the Serbs boycotted the referendum. Let me tell you again, I don't hold it against you that you don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It doesn't seem to me that you have provided the explanation sought by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I will move on, Your Honour. And I move on actually a little in the text, and we move just a few lines further down.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say here: "I myself think the best solution would be a peaceful resolution of the crisis, if Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole became part of Yugoslavia, within the borders that it --" It's page 9. It's just a few lines from the last quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "... within the borders that it has today with all three peoples. In such a case we would not deny the Croatian people the right to leave Yugoslavia and Bosnia and possibly join with Croatia, if they come out for this in a referendum." Mr. Kostic, did you propose here the partition of Bosnia and Herzegovina? That means the part where these Croats live, they join Croatia. Is that what you propose here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, this is not a proposal. How could I make a proposal to a minister from a friendly country in Africa concerning partition and so on? I am only reiterating the unanimous standpoint of the Presidency of the SFRY, which on the 7th of September, 1991, Mr. Mesic presented at the inaugural conference in The Hague. That is to say that we recognise to every constituent nation the right to self-determination, including secession. This is the first of the four principles that Mr. Mesic, on behalf of the entire Presidency, and even all the presidents of the republics, read out at the conference. To this we added the principle that no solutions would be imposed on anybody by force, and the third principle was that all options and all solutions would be treated equally. So I was not making anything up here. This was simply the basis which had previously been accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Can I ask what did you mean, then, would happen if the Croatian people, in a referendum, voted to leave Yugoslavia and Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I cannot say what would have happened if something else had happened. I said that the best solution would be for Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but you go on to say: "In such a case, we would not deny the Croatian people the right to leave Yugoslavia and Bosnia and possibly join with Croatia if they come out for this in a referendum." Now, what did you envisage would happen if the Croatian people decided that's what they wanted to do in a referendum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to tell you that, although I'm not sure, it would have been very difficult to implement, just as I'm sure that voting in a referendum in my country of Montenegro could be carried out peacefully and without any problems. But the principle is always the same and applies to everyone, which is why I advocated the preservation of Yugoslavia and the preservation of Bosnia as a whole within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you are evading the question. There doesn't seem to be within you the ability to talk straight on anything. You have here a clear statement in such a case what you would not deny the Croatian people. You now tell me that that's a bit theoretical and there would be practical difficulties, which may be one or part of the explanation for all the problems that we are dealing with here, but what I would like you to tell me is what you envisaged was the practical way of implementing a decision of the people of Croatia -- the Croatian people in Bosnia, in a referendum, to leave Yugoslavia and Bosnia. How did you envisage that that would be implemented? In fact, in practice, not in theory.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, I cannot provide a precise response to such a hypothetical question. I knew what I was advocating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You raised the question, Mr. Kostic, not me. You raised it in your conversation with the ambassador.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't deny I said it, but I only presented it as a potential possibility based on generally accepted principles within Yugoslavia, principles with which we came to The Hague Conference. We denied no one the right to decide in a democratic manner where and with whom they would live. We only opposed this being done by force, as Croatia and Slovenia did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I simply --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please don't be angry with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. I simply note your unwillingness to answer the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to continue with the document. It's actually a little bit further down on the same page, on page 9. Mr. Nathan Shamuyarira also understood it this way, because he says: "In other words, the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And your answer to him is: "In my opinion, the best solution in this case would probably be for these people in the Serbian Krajina, who wish to remain in within Yugoslavia, to be given the right to self-determination, and the Croats enabled to become part of Croatia along with their territories. That would probably be the least painful solution." Mr. Kostic, you are actually even more clear here on this, what you had in mind. And I would like to make another quote here, because you continue further: "We think that a solution could be reached through political negotiations, that the ethnic majority principle could be applied by agreement, and that could be done by patient negotiations." And then Mr. Shamuyarira says: "Well, let's become get back to division - how would Sarajevo be divided?" And you say: "I do not have a complete picture of how the population is distributed, but the entire area surrounding Sarajevo is populated by Serbs. However, in Sarajevo itself we have all three. The Croats could hardly reckon on being involved in Sarajevo, that's for sure. "But in the event of cantonisation, the Serbs and the Muslims could probably work out how to create a division, as far as Sarajevo is concerned. Because the starting point for cantonisation is the principle of an ethnic majority within a given area. Cantonisation would mean a division of Bosnia and Herzegovina which would allow the Croats and Serbs to have communications and links with their home states, Croatia and Serbia, in other words Yugoslavia." Mr. Kostic, that seems to imply that you had in mind a division, and that would also mean exchange of populations, of resettlement, would it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You are drawing completely the wrong conclusion from all this. At the outset, I said that all my efforts were aimed at preserving Yugoslavia and Bosnia as a whole. Had you allowed us to see a few extracts from this CD that I offered yesterday, Mrs. Dubravka Kenic asked me the same question on the 24th of December, and drew the same conclusion; if there is ethnic division, there is no Bosnia. And I respond that's what it would mean, but it's not the solution. What I see as the solution is for Bosnia as a whole to remain in a common state. All the other possible solutions I mentioned, wasn't that the Cutileiro Plan, the idea to cantonise Bosnia? Weren't all these ideas found in the Dayton peace agreement, madam, and all other peace agreements? Please don't accuse me of wanting to divide Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, I'm not sure I understood how it would necessarily mean the exchange of populations, of resettlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You had put to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- that his position would imply an exchange of populations. Perhaps you could reformulate the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we have heard you say to the ambassador that in 105 of the municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina the Muslims and the Serbs were mixed, and the ethnic majority principle that you refer to here would not work in a 50/50 situation, would it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but in those 105 municipalities, in some places the Muslims were in majority and in others it was the Serbs. And probably the cantonisation envisaged in the Cutileiro Plan would be based on that. It wouldn't have meant resettlement and exchange of populations. Certainly large numbers of people would have remained where they were regardless of whether the canton was to be a Muslim, Serb, or Croatian canton. You know that many Serbs remained in Sarajevo and that even today neither in Republika Srpska nor in the Bosnia-Herzegovina federation do we have an ethnically pure population. In the Croatian federation in Bosnia today, there are Serbs, just as there are Muslims living in Republika Srpska. But these ideas were actually in line with what turned out to be the final peace plan for Bosnia. My biggest mistake -- the Muslims are the most numerous people in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- let me finish my idea. In the former Yugoslavia, the big Yugoslavia, after the Serbs, the Muslims were the most numerous people, scattered in various republics and on various territories, and the biggest mistake I made from the very beginning was that I felt that the Muslims would be the ones advocating preserving the integrity of the entire territory and of the state. Unfortunately, I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, those -- Mr. Kostic, for those who would not want to live -- let's say the Muslims who would not want to live in a Serb territory where 50 per cent had actually -- where the Serbs had the majority but their villages are in there with Muslim majorities, these people, if they didn't want to live on this Serbian territory, would have to leave their homes and go somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend on each individual. We had many large-scale occurrences of individuals of Serb and Croat ethnicity exchanging houses and property and so on, those who didn't want to stay on the territory where they were, but that was their free decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, if you have 105 municipalities in which the population is totally mixed, and where you have, for instance, a 50/50 situation or 55/45 situation, if these people don't want to live, for instance, in the Serb territory, or otherwise in the Muslims' territory, they would have to move, would they not? Your proposal would lead to a change of populations.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What proposal are you talking about? My proposal was to preserve Bosnia in its entirety within Yugoslavia. All this is purely hypothetical, what you're saying. These ideas about a division based on ethnicity, that was found in the Cutileiro Plan. From the very beginning I felt, as I still do today, that the best solution would have been for Bosnia to remain within Yugoslavia as a whole, in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's understood, Mr. Kostic. I was just quoting from your own words, that you had envisioned such a division. And I was just putting to you if that would have been done, that would mean those who don't want to live, for instance, on the Serb territory that you have in mind would have to leave. And that's actually what happened, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I didn't envisage any such division. That's your opinion. You have the right to your opinion, but it's also my right to challenge it and deny it. From the very first day, I advocated Bosnia remaining whole and entire within Yugoslavia, and the ideas you are mentioning were later incorporated into the Cutileiro Plan and the Dayton Accord. Don't expect me to confirm what you're saying. Don't expect to wear me down by your persistent questioning to get me to finally say what you want me to say. As you see, I'm very resilient.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I move on now to another point and it's very brief, actually. The failure to select Mr. Mesic as president of the Presidency, at that time when the Presidency was split and the relations were very tense on the 15th of May, 1991, the regular change on the rotation -- rotating Presidency was supposed to take place. It was the regular procedure; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in the history of the SFRY Presidency, this was always a matter of acclamation, but here in this case, in particular case of Mr. Mesic, that was not that done as before; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. This was by acclamation as well. There was no secret ballot. It was done openly by acclamation at the session. Everyone said openly whether they were for or against. If we have the same understanding as acclamation. There is secret ballot, and then there is voting by acclamation, by the publicly spoken word. At the Presidency, the voting took place by publicly stating one's yea or nay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me then reformulate this. In all the previous Presidency voting for the president, it was not a matter of voting. It was just a matter of agreeing without any vote, and here it was the first time that there was a vote, an official vote. Isn't that how it was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at every session of the Presidency, on the 15th of May when the new president was elected, there was a vote. The only difference and the only problem that arose in this particular case consisted in that this was the first voting on the president of the Presidency in conditions of a multi-party political system which had already been put in place in the republics. Mr. Mesic was elected at multi-party parliamentary elections in Croatia. In conditions of a one-party political system in Yugoslavia, there was a large political body or organisation called The Socialist Alliance of the Working Peoples of Yugoslavia. For the sake of the truth, I have to say that the leadership --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think we are actually straying from the issue. Let me put this to you: At that date in 1991, it was for the Croats to propose the candidate for the president, and they did propose a candidate, and the Serbs -- Serbian leadership and the Montenegrins - actually, we leave them out for the moment - they blocked that, and that was the first time that that ever happened. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
