utterances.text: I said the first time because the first time Mr. Mesic was nominated as a candidate for the Presidency at multi-party elections rather than elections conducted by the Communist Party. In the case of those elections organised by The Socialist Alliance of Working Peoples, every member of the Presidency first had to go through a procedure, and it was the constitutional obligation of every candidate to be a delegate not only of his own republic but all the republics, the entire territory of Yugoslavia. Mr. Mesic did not go through the procedure I mentioned, and there was no way to check his credentials because this body in the meantime had experienced its demise, and for the first time it was up to the Presidency to decide whether to vote for someone who refused to advocate the preservation of Yugoslavia, and that is where this essential difference lay.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This move of yours definitely provoked the Croats and the Croatian leadership, did it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on who you mean among the Croat leadership. We proposed that the Croats offer another candidate who would advocate Yugoslavia rather than an independent Croatia. I personally proposed Mr. Ante Markovic, for example. As I proposed that in this sensitive situation both Croatia and Montenegro waive their positions of president and vice-president and that these be given to Macedonia and another republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not want to go into any more details on this. I will move on to an issue, quite different one. We have already discussed the Defence Exhibit tab 11. That's a statement from a session of the SFRY Presidency regarding events in Croatia, and it's on the 4th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 4th of May, yes. What did I say? I said 4th of May.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm not -- I wasn't in the Presidency then.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no, but you discussed this tab 11, you discussed this with Mr. Milosevic, and I just want to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- to refer to it briefly, because in this -- on -- in the second paragraph -- yes, in the second paragraph, it says here: "The SFRY Presidency opined that the most recent events in the Knin Krajina and Eastern Slavonia, and in particular the tragic events in Borovo Selo, had demonstrated all the complexity of the political and security situation in the country which threatens to escalate into large-scale ethnic conflict which has brought the country to the brink of civil war." And it says here specifically, "The SFRY Presidency expressed its regret at the large number of casualties." Mr. Kostic, in Borovo Selo there were casualties on both sides. In particular, 12 Croat policemen were killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you remember the fact that 12 Croatian policemen were killed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that detail, but I know that several Croatian policemen were killed. I don't know if there were 12 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We heard quite some evidence related to the events in Borovo Selo from May 1991, and we had in particular here witnesses like Mr. Babic, Jovan Dulovic, a person C-013, B-129, and C-047 testify about the events. The witness C-013, for instance, said that there were clashes between Croatian police and armed Serbs, including volunteers from the SRS Party from Serbia. Is that what you know about? Do you know that, too, that Seselj's men were involved?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Babic, Milan Babic, told us that two of Seselj's volunteers were killed. Do you know about these two casualties?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I know is that because of the events in Borovo Selo, we had 8.000 refugees. And that was my motive, the motive that prompted me to go and visit there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Babic also mentioned that Frenki Simatovic and his men were involved in Borovo Selo. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that. I wasn't in the Presidency at the time, so I wasn't called upon as a member of the Presidency of the Supreme Command. It was only later when I was elected to the Presidency that I felt the responsibility and need to visit first and foremost the refugees, which were refugees because of the events in Borovo Selo, and I made a public statement on the occasion and said that that mustn't be only a problem of Serbia and Croatia but it must be taken as being the problem of the whole of the Yugoslav community. Therefore, a problem of the Presidency and the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, did you visit Borovo Selo in May 1991, when these tragic events occurred, or only in July?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't visit then. It was in July when I was visited.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you recall when exactly did you visit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I also have some footage of that visit. I couldn't tell you a precise date now, madam, because it's been 15 years since then. So I wouldn't hazard a guess as to the date. But I do know that it was just before the election of the president of the state commission for the cease-fire and that Mr. Mesic, at the Presidency, was categorically opposed to my election precisely because I had visited Borovo Selo. And when I was elected president of that state commission, gaining agreement from the other members of the Presidency, Mr. Mesic in a demonstrative manner left the Presidency session, walked out. Now, if the date is very important to you, I'll do my best to find it and tell you subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually enough to clarify that it was quite immediately before this session that you just mentioned. That's -- that's enough to clarify it. But I --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, before the meeting. Immediately before the meeting.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to play now to you that -- we are now using Sanction to play three clips from your visit in Borovo Selo, and we have here the transcript of what you said there. And we --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia, Branko Kostic, visited Borovo Selo. In talking to the inhabitants, Kostic said that the defenders cannot be called terrorists or bandits. He criticised the federal government because, as he said, there was insufficient assistance given to the people, and positively assessed the JNA. 'You can count on -- the fact that they call you Chetniks and terrorists is not founded,' stressed Kostic. 'We are just a self-organised armed people.' According to Branko Kostic, the secessionist policy of Croatia and Slovenia cannot be tolerated and accepted because if we were to accept such unilateral acts, in Europe there could be at least 70 new states coming into existence." THE PROSECUTOR: Yes. And can we just have the next clip, and then pause after.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] As you can see, dear viewers, Branko Kostic, the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, has visited Borovo Selo and several thousand inhabitants."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters apologise but they can't find the actual transcript so they're doing a live interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I was in a sacred place yesterday, Vucji Dol, important for our history, and I consider you here the followers of those heroes who were always ready throughout our history to defend their own thresholds and their own freedom. Persevere and be brave. "Some of the people that I work with now, and you know who I mean, are referring to you as renegades, Chetniks, terrorists, whereas I always say to them the renegades are those who violated the Yugoslav constitution and enacted unilateral acts and not you here who are fighting for that constitution and for Yugoslavia. "Mr. Kostic said what was important. The most important thing was what he said at the end: That you can rest assured that you are not alone, and if you are bandits, then there are other bandits who will come to defend and protect you."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's pause here. Mr. Kostic, you just said a minute ago that you were not aware that there were any volunteers, Seselj volunteers, or members from the SRS party there, and now you refer in both of these clips to Chetniks, that they are referring to you as Chetniks, but Chetniks, that's the Seselj's men, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, you are showing complete ignorance now; ignorance of terms, ignorance of names. The Croats called anybody who any -- anything to do with the S of Serbia or Serbhood and Serbdom were Chetniks. They referred to members of the Yugoslav People's Army as Chetniks, and the Territorial Defence, and the volunteers, and the paramilitaries. The Croats referred to all of those people with one term; the Chetniks. That's why I say you show complete ignorance of terminology. Now, the term "Chetnik" and "Chetniks" was used bring Mr. Stjepan Mesic as president of the Presidency at official Yugoslav state Presidency meetings. I heard him say it. I listened to him say it once, twice, three times, and then I finally said, "Mr. Mesic, you're the president of Yugoslavia and you cannot refer to those people as Chetniks, terrorists and bandits, because you are Chetniks, terrorists, and bandits if you are treading on the Yugoslav constitution and wanting to arrive at an independent state by your own means." And that's the truth, madam. Now, how come Seselj has anything to do with this here now?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. -- Mr. Kostic, this Brane Crncevic that spoke after you, he is who? What is his position and why was he coming with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brane Crncevic was a respected writer, Serbian writer, but he didn't go with me in his capacity as writer but he went with me, unless I'm much mistaken, as a man who was in charge of the refugees in the Serbian government. I think -- well, I don't know if it was the ministry, a ministry of some kind or some committee for displaced persons and refugees, but that's how he came to be there with me. But if you're asking me about him personally, my views, my political views and ideology, they diverge quite a bit from his.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please now have the third clip.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] After a hearty welcome in the centre of Borovo Selo, the vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, Branko Kostic, had talks with the leadership of the Serb autonomous province or area of Western Srem and Slavonia. Hadzic informed him of the situation in the area. "The people here are not Chetniks, terrorists, and bandits. They are the Serb people and I can say that they are part of the Croatian people as well, because there are some Croats there up at the barricade with us that do not recognise the Ustasha authority and do not want to live through the genocide of 50 years ago. "Branko Kostic also said that we have a republishing of the ideology that we saw 50 years ago. "The world and Europe remembered that sort of policy very well, and I am convinced that Europe and the world at large will finally come to realise today too what that policy and those politics means and what terrible consequences such a policy can have, not only on the Serb people themselves living in this area of Croatia, which are the ones most immediately threatened, but also consequences that such a policy could have further afield in Europe as well. Our federal organs, especially the Federal Executive Council, up until now have not been on a par with the job ahead of them because it was through force of circumstance that we're dealing with an area under jeopardy where the Serb people are suffering. And it is the efforts of the Federal Executive Council in this case and in other cases that must be expressed in full measure and materially viewed as well, regardless of the ethnic composition of the population which is undergoing these hardships. We shall do everything in our power to ensure that that Yugoslav People's Army of ours, which is a strong army, a powerful army, and which has the wherewithal -- more than ever before to give assistance --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we have to adjourn in a minute or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it is actually -- we are almost at the end. It's actually the end.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] All parts of the population who are under threat or are already being jeopardised, regardless of where they are. The today it is the Serb people in Croatia that are under threat. Now, if developments follow the course that none of us would like to see, we don't exclude the possibility of certain other --"

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually a little bit further than I wanted it to be played.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for playing that footage. Thank you for showing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually already an exhibit. It's part of the videos that were tendered as Exhibit 352, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will have to -- regrettably we will have to put off your question on that clip for tomorrow morning -- not tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Actually, next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But Mr. Kostic knows, and I think I can ask the questions. We need not have it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. He remembered the clip. He thanked you for playing it, after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would actually like Your Honours, just that Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- constitutions of Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, and they're also to be passed on to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Passed on, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are adjourned until next Monday at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Courtroom 1, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of February, 2006, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
